question_text: Draw the switch node voltage waveform in an asynchronous buck converter alongside the high-side gate control signal. How does it change if it is synchronous?
answer_text: When the gate is HIGH, the switch node jumps to V_in. When LOW, it drops slightly below ground (-V_f of the diode). In a synchronous buck, it drops exactly to 0V.
explanation_text: The switch node toggles between the input voltage and ground. In an async converter, the diode must conduct during the OFF time. To forward-bias the diode, the inductor's flyback pulls the switch node to roughly -0.7V. In a sync converter, the low-side MOSFET turns on and provides a near-zero resistance path, keeping the node perfectly at 0V (aside from a tiny I * R_DS(on) drop).
bonus_question_text: What happens at the switch node during the "dead time" of a synchronous buck converter?
bonus_answer_text: Both FETs are off, so the internal body diode of the low-side FET takes over. The switch node briefly dips to -0.7V just like an asynchronous converter until the low-side FET fully turns on.
